scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Saqra originated in the late 19th century in the province of Paucartambo, located within the Cusco Region of Peru.
Its visual and thematic creation was directly inspired by sacred paintings of Mamacha Carmen, the local name for the Virgen del Carmen.
In Quechua, saqra translates to malignant, restless, or mischievous, describing a devilish entity that, unlike Supay, focuses on performing innocent tricks.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Saqra is performed at religious feasts honoring patron saints, most notably Mamacha Carmen in Paucartambo and the Virgen del Rosario de Huallhua in the San Salvador District of the Calca Province.
The dance represents mischievous agility and harmless devilry within a sacred festive setting.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers dress as animal figures using elaborate masks and attire.
In the Vilcanota Valley variant (Saqra León), the costume is finely ordered and predominantly features lion imagery, accompanied by a feather crown, mirrors, decorations, and a whip (chicote).

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Saqra is sibling of Ch'unchu: Co-exists in the same Paucartambo festival cycle for Mamacha Carmen.
Saqra is sibling of Qhapaq negro: Performed alongside Saqra at patron saint festivals in Cusco.
Saqra is sibling of Qhapaq Qulla: Shares the Paucartambo feast setting and highland traditional context.
